analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to give the military the parts, tools, and manuals to repair its own equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in December 2024, referred to the Armed Services Committee, and received no hearing, vote, or cosponsors before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require defense contractors to give the Department of Defense 'fair and reasonable access' to the parts, tools, and technical information needed to diagnose, maintain, and repair the equipment it buys. It would also make the military log every instance where troops could not fix equipment because a contractor controlled the repair, and publish annual reports on those cases. The aim is to cut maintenance costs and keep equipment mission-ready without waiting on the manufacturer.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund an estimated hundreds of billions in defense operating and support costs each year and could see savings when the military can repair its own gear instead of paying the manufacturer or shipping equipment back to contractor facilities. Servicemembers also benefit: crews could fix broken equipment on site and get back to training or operations instead of waiting weeks for a contractor visit.

how_it_helps.text: Contracts could not be awarded unless the contractor agrees in writing to provide the Department of Defense fair and reasonable access to the parts, tools, and information used to diagnose, maintain, or repair the good or service, on terms no worse than what authorized repair shops get [S2].
The bill adds cost-saving proposals to every acquisition strategy, including projected dollar savings and their time frame, and requires the Pentagon to publicly report on them [S2].

It directs the military to establish a system for servicemembers to log right-to-repair obstructions — cases where a contractor's conditions forced troops to ship equipment away, wait for a contractor visit, or scrap usable gear — and to publish an annual public report summarizing them [S2].
It expands the military's rights in technical data to cover diagnosis and repair, and directs a government review of how failing to acquire sufficient intellectual property raises support costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors that currently hold exclusive control over repair parts, diagnostic tools, and technical data for military equipment. They would have to share those materials on demand at no better-than-authorized-repairer terms, giving up a profitable monopoly on servicing equipment they sell to the government.

drawbacks.text: Sharing repair materials on government-set terms could reduce contractors' aftermarket service revenue, and opponents of right-to-repair mandates for defense equipment have argued this could lead contractors to raise upfront prices or decline to bid on certain programs (a general policy argument; the provided sources contain no statement of opposition) [S2].

The bill's savings are projections: it requires cost-saving proposals with a 'likelihood of achieving the savings' but does not itself guarantee any dollar amount, and its own structure — a report on cost savings, a GAO compliance report — acknowledges the actual impact must be measured after the fact [S2].

Contractors could argue the requirement touches intellectual property they developed at private expense, and the bill addresses this only by directing an evaluation of cost-effectiveness rather than resolving the underlying IP dispute [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit case is strong on its face: the military already owns the equipment, and being locked out of repairing it means paying a manufacturer to do work troops could do themselves, sometimes at the cost of mission readiness. The main cost is to contractors' service revenue and possibly higher upfront bids, and the honest answer is that the bill relies on annual reports and GAO audits to prove the savings rather than establishing them in advance. Even a partial success would likely save taxpayers far more than it costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 12, 2024, and sent to the Armed Services Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Servicemember Right-to-Repair Act of 2024 in the Senate on December 12, 2024 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services the same day; no further action was ever taken [S4].
No senator cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list shows zero [S3].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2025, ending the 118th Congress, so the bill died in committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors keep their exclusive control over military equipment repair — and keep charging the Pentagon for parts, tools, and contractor-performed maintenance — since the requirement was never enacted. The bill's timing (introduced in the final weeks of a Congress) and lack of cosponsors meant it never had a realistic path, so the outcome mostly preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defense contractors who monopolize repair work

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate; it was her only direct action before referral.

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee (Chair Jack Reed)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 12, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Defense contractors and aerospace manufacturers
against.role: Industry holding exclusive repair rights over military equipment
against.what_they_did: The industry has broadly resisted right-to-repair requirements in defense contracting; no industry opposition to this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so its support never took a measurable partisan shape.

industries.note: These companies sell the Pentagon equipment and then control the repair chain — the parts, tools, and technical data — charging the government for contractor-performed maintenance. The bill would require them to share those materials on fair terms, cutting into a profitable aftermarket monopoly that ordinary taxpayers pay for.

Some contractor logistics firms would gain access to repair materials on equal terms, potentially competing for repair work they are currently locked out of. Servicemembers and military maintenance crews would gain faster, cheaper repairs.
